{{c|''To {{ls}}hevv how through Gods grace the Iewes {{ls}}halbe ouerrunne of the Gentils, although they beginne after, he bringeth a parable of men working {{ls}}oner and later in the vineyard, but the later revvarded in the end euen as the fir{{ls}}t. 17 He reuealeth more to his Di{{ls}}ciples touching his pa{{ls}}sion: 20 Bidding the ambitious tvvo {{ls}}uiters to thinke rather of {{ls}}uffering with him: 24 And teaching vs (in the re{{ls}}t of his Di{{ls}}ciples) not to be greeued at our Eccle{{ls}}ia{{ls}}tical Superiors, con{{ls}}idering they are (as he was him {{ls}}elf) to toile for our Saluation. 29 Then going out of Iericho, he geueth {{ls}}ight vnto tvvo blind.''}}

{{dropinitial|T|fl={{verse|chapter=20|verse=1}}}}{{sc|He}} {{MarginNote|margin=left|margin-width=65|text=The Go{{ls}}pel vpon the Sunday of Septuage{{ls}}me.}}kingdom of heauen is like to a man that is an hou{{ls}}holder vvhich vvēt forth early {{sup|‖}} in the morning to hire vvorkemen into his vineyard. {{verse|chapter=20|verse=2}} And hauing made couenāt vvith the Workemen for a penie a day, he {{ls}}ent them into his vineyard. {{verse|chapter=20|verse=3}} And going forth about the third houre, he {{ls}}avv other {{ls}}tanding in the market place idle, {{verse|chapter=20|verse=4}} and he {{ls}}aid to them, Goe you al{{ls}}o into the vineyard: and that vvhich {{ls}}hal be iu{{ls}}t, I vvil giue you. {{verse|chapter=20|verse=5}} And they vvent their vvay. And againe he vvent forth about the {{ls}}ixt & the ninth houre: and did likevvi{{ls}}e. {{verse|chapter=20|verse=6}} But about the eleuenth houre he vvent forth and found other {{ls}}tanding, & he {{ls}}aith to them, What {{ls}}tand you here al the day idle? {{verse|chapter=20|verse=7}} They {{ls}}ay to him, Becau{{ls}}e no man hath hired vs. He {{ls}}aith to them, Goe you al{{ls}}o into the vineyard.

{{verse|chapter=20|verse=8}} And vvhen euening vvas come, the lord of the vineyard {{ls}}aith to his bailife, Call the vvorkemen, and pay them their hire, beginning from the la{{ls}}t euen to the fir{{ls}}t. {{verse|chapter=20|verse=9}} Therfore vvhen they vvere come that came about the eleuenth houre, they receiued euery one a {{sup|‖}} penie. {{verse|chapter=20|verse=10}} But vvhen the fir{{ls}}t al{{ls}}o came, they thought that they {{ls}}hould receiue more: and they al{{ls}}o receiued euery one a penie. {{verse|chapter=20|verse=11}} And receiuing it they {{MarginNote|margin=left|margin-width=65|text=∷ The Iewes are noted for enuying the vocation of the Gentiles, and their reward equal with thē {{ls}}elues.}}∷ murmured again{{ls}}t the good man of the hou{{ls}}e, {{verse|chapter=20|verse=12}} {{ls}}aying, The{{ls}}e la{{ls}}t haue continued one houre: and thou ha{{ls}}t made them equal to vs that haue borne the burden of the day and the heates. {{verse|chapter=20|verse=13}} But he an{{ls}}vvering {{ls}}aid to one of them, Frende, I doe the no vvrong: did{{ls}}t thou not couenant vvith me for a penie? {{verse|chapter=20|verse=14}} Take that is thine, and goe: I vvil al{{ls}}o giue to this la{{ls}}t euen as to thee al{{ls}}o. {{verse|chapter=20|verse=15}} Or, is it not lavvful for me to do that I vvil? is thine eye naught, becau{{ls}}e I am good? {{verse|chapter=20|verse=16}} So {{ls}}hal the la{{ls}}t, be fir{{ls}}t: and the fir{{ls}}t, la{{ls}}t. For many be called, but {{sup|‖}} fevv elect.⊣
